related_questions.snippet: Common side effects include pain at the injection site, fever, body aches and headaches. These reactions are frequent (and indicate that your body is making an immune response to the vaccine) and should go away within 1-2 days, with the exception that swollen lymph nodes may persist up to about 10 days.

related_questions.question: How long to wait between vaccines?

text_blocks.snippet: Generally, for most vaccines, there isn't a strict minimum waiting time between doses when administered on separate occasions. However, specific guidelines apply to live vaccines. If two different live injectable or nasal vaccines are not administered on the same day, they should be separated by at least 4 weeks. If they are given less than 4 weeks apart, the second vaccine should be repeated at least 4 weeks after the invalid dose.
snippet_highlighted_words: If two different live injectable or nasal vaccines are not administered on the same day, they should be separated by at least 4 weeks

list.snippet: Same Day: Live vaccines (like MMR or varicella) can be given on the same day.
Separate Days: If not given on the same day, there should be at least 4 weeks between doses of live injectable or nasal vaccines.
Less Than 4 Weeks Apart: If live vaccines are administered less than 4 weeks apart, the second one is considered invalid and should be repeated at least 4 weeks after the invalid dose.

list.title: No Minimum:
list.snippet: For most other vaccines (non-live), there isn't a strict minimum waiting time between doses when administered at separate visits, according to Penn Medicine.

list.title: Same Visit:
list.snippet: Multiple vaccines (including live and non-live) can be administered at the same visit, says Cleveland Clinic Health Essentials.

list.title: Specifics:
list.snippet: Some vaccines, like the hepatitis B series, have specific minimum intervals between doses, but these are generally outlined in the vaccination schedule.

list.title: Individual Needs:
list.snippet: It's crucial to consult with a healthcare provider to determine the most appropriate vaccination schedule based on individual health status and needs, according to the CDC.

list.title: Interrupted Schedules:
list.snippet: If a vaccination schedule is interrupted, it's generally not necessary to restart the entire series, but the healthcare provider will advise on the best way to complete it.

list.title: Sick Individuals:
list.snippet: If someone is sick with a moderate or severe acute illness, they should wait until they recover before getting vaccinated, says the CDC.
